The camera moving backward along its line of sight increases the distance to all objects, but since the blue cylinder is the only object being tracked for depth variation in the grid, and assuming uniform scaling, the relative depth distribution remains similar. However, because the entire scene recedes, the absolute depth values increase. Since the object doesn’t change shape or orientation, the internal depth gradient (from front face to back face) remains the same — just scaled up.

But note: the instruction says “depth of the blue cylinder's surface in that cell relative to the average depth over all of its covered cells”. So if the whole object moves farther away uniformly, the *relative* depths (i.e., differences from the mean) remain unchanged. Therefore, the pattern of depth values across the grid should be identical to what it would be if the object were at original position — because we’re measuring relative to the new average depth.

Since the camera moves backward along its line of sight (which is roughly perpendicular to the image plane, i.e., zooming out), the apparent size of the cylinder decreases slightly, but its position in the image grid remains centered horizontally and vertically in the same region. The shape and coverage pattern on the 32x32 grid will be nearly identical — perhaps slightly smaller due to perspective, but for simplicity and given the low resolution, we can assume the coverage mask is unchanged.

For example, if originally the front face was at depth D_avg - Δ, and back face at D_avg + Δ, after moving back by δ, they become (D_avg + δ) - Δ and (D_avg + δ) + Δ, so the difference from the new average (D_avg + δ) is still -Δ and +Δ.
